newsitem.title: ITALY: Timing of Italy rate cut is surprise-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Timing of Italy rate cut is surprise-analysts.

text.p: The timing of a 75 basis point reduction in Italy's discount rate to 7.50 percent on Wednesday took analysts by surprise and left the way open to a further reduction by the year end, economists said.
"The size of the move and the fact that they would make a cut was expected," said Sally Wilkinson, at UBS in London.

"The timing was very unexpected...It looks like they brought things forward. I expect the Bank of Italy will reward the government if they get the budget through and I think we could see seven percent by the end of the year."
Lorenzo Codogno at Bank of America said the reduction was "probably the first of a series of cuts" and expected the move to go down well in the markets.
Btp/bund yield futures held steady immediately after the cut, but 10-year bonds later firmed to 105.02 from 104.75 around the close. Btp futures firmed to 123.70 from closing levels around 123.46.
The lira showed little initial reaction but later tumbled against the mark to creep towards the 1,006 level.
"We can't completely rule out a small reduction before the end of the year, but we definitely expect a bigger cut by next summer," economist said Claudio Tosato of Deutsche Bank.

Analysts said the speed of the move may have reflected concerns over an economic slowdown. They had been widely expecting the Bank of Italy to cut rates by 75-100 basis points in about a month's time, provided passage of the 1997 austerity budget was on track.

"The advance in the timing reflects concern over the economy. It's been flat and it was probably flat in the third quarter and it's showing only mild signs of a pickup," said an economist with a U.S. investment bank in London.

The move, which came after markets closed, followed upbeat preliminary consumer prices data from 10 Italian sample cities on Monday and Tuesday which pointed to an October inflation rate of 3.0 percent year-on-year, against 3.4 percent in September.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio had set three percent inflation as the target to be reached before rates would be cut.
Francesco Giordano at San Paolo, one of the few analysts expecting the Bank to move earlier rather than later, applauded the Bank's policy of trimming rates when goals were achieved.

"The Bank had a window of opportunity...If German rates go up, it will be difficult for the Bank of Italy to cut much more," he said, noting comments earlier by Bundesbank board member Otmar Issing quashing hopes of further German rate cuts.
But Giordano added: "It's likely that we'll see another 50 basis point cut before the end of the year to celebrate approval of the budget."
